statements.quote: This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.
During the diagnostic phase, students were asked to complete an online questionnaire aimed at collecting information about their perception of their own creative abilities.

For this study, a printed template was used to allow students to list uses for a particular object; in this case, the object tire was selected. The session was led by a facilitator (first author) and lasted approximately 15 minutes, with a general introduction explaining the purpose, a total of 3 minutes for the exercise, and the collection of templates and closing remarks.

Students were given a printed brief stating the design task, with the indication to generate various ideas and detail a few of them, as well as instructions for the documentation of results. The design task was: how can we promote conscious water use in the home by its inhabitants? No specific context was given.
statements.locator: p. 4, Section 3.2.2, Second Phase: implementation of a design task

statements.quote: The four groups were instructed to document their process and upload the results to an online folder. AI groups were asked to include all conversations and image results in a document, while sketch groups were asked to photograph their sketches, including annotations. Upon task completion, students within each group responded a questionnaire about the perception of the exercise and their results.

Evaluators first received a document with the data and later participated in a session to discuss instructions for the rating. The first author of the study created a PDF document which included image results (whether sketch or AI) and the text of the concepts or prompt describing the image. Each participant received a number to ensure the participant’s anonymity. Only ideas that were developed on image level with an explanatory description were included in the document. In the case of AI groups, images that were too abstract or far away from a concrete idea (and that the students themselves discarded) were not included. As AI generates many image variations on the same idea, all these were included, but were considered one concept for rating. A total of 71 ideas for the sketch group (n=31 students) and 44 ideas for the AI groups (n=30 students) were included in the PDF document.

To analyze the design space exploration and framing, as well as the evolution of design intent within participants’ creative processes, we followed a systematic approach. This involved studying all documents uploaded by students and comparing the problemsolution space and design “moves” with sketches and AI images. This information was then translated into a graphical analysis to identify distinct exploration patterns. Additionally, we conducted a thematic analysis for the initial prompt per participant within AI groups to understand different prompting styles.

In terms of diversity, each participant’s total ideas were documented in an Excel table and then sorted into recurring themes and counted. The classification was based on final categories, which were determined by the focus of the proposed idea or framing of the problem.

1. Studying all documents uploaded by students (annotated sketches and AI dialogue logs + images in PDF format). 

2. Analyzing each case, identifying exploration strategies. For the AI group, we analyzed the complete conversation log, registering each prompt and following AI answer within problem and solution space, as well as image generation within the LLM, prompt generation by the LLM for image generation in an external TTI Model, and switching models. For the sketch group, we analyzed written notes accompanying the sketches, that show the reasoning process of the designer. 

3. Coding of moves/sequence within problem and solution space in Excel, assigning values to codes. 

4. Visualizing data for each participant, translating values in Excel to symbols.

For the first phase, familiarization, the main researcher read through the students uploaded conversation log. Upon examination, 3 reports were discarded since they were not complete or did not include enough information for analysis. The remaining 27 logs were analyzed, and the initial and subsequent prompts were documented in an annotated Excel table. Based on this, the main researcher scanned for initial codes and themes. These were reviewed with the second researcher and a refinement on final themes was agreed upon.

The authors would like to thank lecturers Héctor López, Triana Martínez, Annika Maya, Miguel de Paz, and Ramsés Viazcán for their support in carrying out the exploratory study and related research activities, and student Miranda Moyo for assistance in organizing image results.

notes: Checked on 2026-10-09. Read the complete 75323-character markdown (473 lines) and checked relevant passages against the 14-page PDF, including Acknowledgments and references; there is no appendix and the PDF contains no embedded attachments. No public-data, code-release, preregistration, supplementary-file, or data-on-request statement was found. IBM SPSS Statistics is mentioned as analysis software, without a script or code location. The quoted statements describe study materials and records collected or used internally; none grants public access. The online folder, participant-numbered rating PDF, and Excel tables have no URL. Both data_url and code_url in forms/c112.json are empty. PDF hyperlinks contain article/reference links, author identifiers, licensing and author contacts, with no research-data repository link. Bibliographic references to other papers were not treated as deposits for this study. The paper's CC BY 4.0 statement licenses the article and does not establish a license for unlocated underlying data. Publisher check: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3772318.3791350 returned HTTP 403 with a Cloudflare 'Just a moment...' bot check; stopped without attempting to bypass it. Thus publisher supplementary files could not be verified. https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791350 requested with Accept: application/json,text/html;q=0.9 returned HTTP 200 after content-negotiation redirect to https://api.crossref.org/v1/works/10.1145%2F3772318.3791350/transform. The metadata has an empty relation object and only an article PDF in link; this is not evidence that publisher supplementary files do not exist. DataCite, Zenodo, Harvard Dataverse and OSF searches were completed by title and first-author name, with shorter-title and DOI searches as detailed above. The Zenodo author match is a different Gemini/STEEPLE future-scenario study and contains only its article PDF; it is not c112 data. No relevant deposit was identified, so deposits is empty; no rows, columns, assignments, scores, or complete idea corpus could be inspected. No data files were downloaded. For S1, the missing ratings linked to participant and assigned group in final.open_items remain unavailable, preventing calculation from public records of per-person creativity means, arm SDs/SEs, or uncertainty accounting for both the four randomized groups and multiple ideas per student. Public records also cannot resolve the conflicting group letters, intended standardized effect/interval, or the unexplained baseline AUT participant counts. Individual fluency/flexibility scores and complete texts/ideas are likewise unavailable for recomputation of participant-level dispersion or diversity. The printed aggregate results, selected images, and example prompts are insufficient for these analyses. Status none_found describes the completed search, not proof that no deposit exists. Confidence is medium because the publisher landing page could not be inspected and unlinked or differently titled deposits could be missed. No access request, account creation, or login was attempted.
